title: Bandi Chhor Divas
hook: lamps are lit to remember Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior, at Diwali time

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan's martyrdom day, and a cup of cold water on a hot road. Your line was cool water for anyone. Today, a night of lamps.

Autumn, and across much of India the lamps come out. Diwali: rows of little clay lamps on windowsills, fireworks, boxes of sweets passed over walls to the neighbors. Hindus light them for Rama coming home, and for Lakshmi. Jains light them for Mahavira. On the same nights, Sikhs light lamps too, for a story of their own, one you've already heard on this path: a prison, a Guru who wouldn't leave alone, and a cloak.
screen: `LAMPS ON EVERY WINDOWSILL.` → `THE SAME NIGHTS, DIFFERENT STORIES.` → `A PRISON, AND A CLOAK.`

segments.voice: The day is called Bandi Chhor Divas. Bandi means a prisoner, chhor means to set free, divas is day: the day of the one who freed the prisoners. On day sixty-seven you heard the story. Tradition says Guru Hargobind, held by the emperor Jahangir in the fort at Gwalior, would not leave without the fifty-two rajas imprisoned with him, and walked out with every one of them holding a tassel of his cloak. Today is how the Sikh year keeps it. Sikhs remember that when he reached Amritsar, people lit lamps to welcome him, and it was Diwali time. So the day moves with Diwali, each autumn. At the Harmandir Sahib, that evening is the great one of the year. Ledges, railings and walkways are lined with lamps and strings of light, the whole building shimmers on the water, and fireworks open over the pool. A Punjabi saying puts it simply: dal and roti at home, but Diwali in Amritsar. At home, families set little lamps along walls and windowsills, share sweets, and go to the gurdwara. And inside the Gwalior fort itself there is now a gurdwara, called Data Bandi Chhor, where the Guru is remembered at the place he was held. Notice what all those lamps are for. Not an escape. A refusal to be free alone. The Guru's own release was a door, and he held it open until everyone behind him was through. And on those nights, Sikh and Hindu lamps burn on neighboring windowsills, each for its own story.
screen: `BANDI — PRISONER. CHHOR — SET FREE.` · `THE CLOAK, FROM DAY SIXTY-SEVEN.` · `DAL AND ROTI AT HOME, DIWALI IN AMRITSAR.` · `NOT FREE ALONE.` · then, large: `BANDI CHHOR.`

segments.voice: If there's a candle or a tea light nearby and it's safe, light it; if not, picture one, small and steady, a little flicker at the top. In its light, hold someone who got free of something, out of a hospital, a bad job, a hard year, a debt, a cell, and right beside them anyone you know who is still waiting to get free. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
Bandi Chhor. The liberator of prisoners: a name for Guru Hargobind, who would not leave the fort at Gwalior without the fifty-two.
Your line: light for the freed. Fifty-two rajas, one cloak, and every one of them free. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Bandi Chhor Divas, which falls at Diwali time, Sikhs light lamps and candles at home and in gurdwaras; the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated and fireworks are set off over its pool.

fork.setup: Diwali night in Amritsar, and Sikhs are lighting lamps around the Harmandir Sahib. what are they remembering?
options: a Guru coming home after he freed the prisoners.
fork.reveal: Guru Hargobind's return from Gwalior with the fifty-two rajas. their Hindu neighbors, on the same nights, light lamps for Rama coming home.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the releaser of prisoners, a title for Guru Hargobind.
